pronoun noun

in grammar

also pronouns, personal pronoun, intensive pronoun, indefinite pronoun, definite pronoun

classical

Quint. 1.5.47: prōnōmen quoque genus, numerum, cāsūs habet
Varr. LL 8.45; Quint. 1.4.19 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 220, 223, 248, 366

prōnōmen, prōnōminis n.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

a pronoun

The word that stands “for a noun”, prō nōmine: Traupman’s pupil defines it as pars ōrātiōnis quae prō nōmine pōnitur (Traupman 223). The kinds have the grammarians’ names, mostly late: a personal pronoun is prōnōmen persōnāle, a relative relātīvum, an interrogative interrogātīvum, a reflexive reciprocum (Priscian), a possessive possessīvum (Quint. 1.5.45), and a demonstrative dēmōnstrātīvum (Traupman 224); see those words. Traupman’s prōnōmen intentiōnis for an intensive pronoun (ipse) is not found in Lewis & Short. Varro calls the indefinite pronoun articulus īnfīnītus (Lewis & Short s.v. īnfīnītus).

Other words

  • prōvocābulum, prōvocābulī n. — a pronoun, “a word used for another word”

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Auct. ap. Varr. LL 8.45 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    An early grammarian’s word, cited by Varro; prōnōmen prevailed.

Examples

  • prōnōmen quoque genus, numerum, cāsūs habet

    the pronoun too has gender, number and caseQuint. 1.5.47

  • Prōnōmen quid est?

    What is a pronoun?Traupman 223
